description: Software testing principles, test types, TDD/BDD, test design and edge-case techniques, and verification practices for coding agents. For an engineer/architect who sets testing strategy and works with AI agents.

notes.front: Dijkstra's limit on testing, and its practical lesson?
notes.back: "Testing can show the presence of bugs, but never their absence." A green suite is evidence, not proof.
notes.extra: Same as ISTQB principle 1; motivates formal methods, property tests and humility about coverage.

notes.back: Debugging: find and fix the cause of a known failure (make it run). Testing: check that it solves the problem and find unknown failures.

notes.front: Why did Myers define a successful test as one that finds a bug?
notes.back: Testers aiming to show software works pick inputs that pass; aiming to break it finds the defects.
notes.extra: Definition: testing is executing a program with the intent of finding errors (The Art of Software Testing).

notes.back: Verification: building the product right (meets spec)? Validation: building the right product (meets user needs)?
notes.analogy: Verification checks the house matches the blueprint; validation checks the family actually wants to live in it.

notes.text: A human {{c1::error}} (mistake) introduces a {{c2::fault}} (defect/bug) in the code, which causes a {{c3::failure}} (observable wrong behaviour) only when executed under the right conditions.

notes.back: Knowing what the correct output is. Without an oracle a test can only check "didn't crash".
notes.analogy: Grading an exam with no answer key: you can only check the student wrote something.
notes.extra: Mitigations: properties/invariants, differential testing, metamorphic relations, golden files, human review.

notes.text: ISTQB's seven testing principles: testing shows {{c1::presence, not absence}} of defects; {{c2::exhaustive testing}} is impossible; {{c3::early testing}} saves time and money; defects {{c4::cluster together}}; tests wear out (the {{c5::pesticide paradox}}); testing is {{c6::context dependent}}; the {{c7::absence-of-defects}} fallacy.

notes.back: Re-running the same tests stops finding new bugs: they only probe the paths they were written for. Refresh suites and add new techniques.
notes.analogy: Spraying the same field the same way: the pests that survive are exactly the ones the spray never reaches.

notes.back: A system with no known bugs can still be useless if it doesn't meet user needs: validation matters as much as verification.
Shift-left: test earlier (requirements, design, CI), where defects are cheaper. Shift-right: test and observe in production (canaries, flags, chaos).

notes.front: Black-box vs white-box vs grey-box testing?
notes.back: Black: from the spec, no internals. White: from code structure (branches, paths). Grey: partial knowledge (schema, architecture).
Static: examine without executing (reviews, linters, type checks, SAST). Dynamic: execute the code.
Functional: does it do the right thing (features, rules)? Non-functional: how well (performance, security, usability, reliability)?
A fast, deterministic test of a small unit in isolation. Classicists mean a unit of behaviour (possibly several classes), not one class.
Checks components work together. Narrow: one boundary (service + real DB via Testcontainers). Broad: many live services at once.
The consumer records its expectations of a provider's API as a contract; the provider verifies it in its own CI. Catches breaking changes without full E2E. Tool: Pact.
notes.analogy: The consumer hands the provider a checklist; the provider ticks it off before every release.

notes.back: Full user journey through the deployed stack. Highest confidence per test, but slowest, flakiest and costliest: keep few, on critical paths.
notes.extra: Tools: Playwright, Cypress.

notes.back: System: the whole integrated system against its requirements. Acceptance (UAT): does it meet business/user acceptance criteria, often owned by business.
Smoke: shallow, broad check that a build is alive before deeper testing. Sanity: narrow, quick check that a specific fix works.
notes.analogy: Smoke test: switch the device on and see whether smoke comes out.

notes.back: Re-running tests to check that changes didn't break existing behaviour.

notes.text: Performance tests: {{c1::load}} = expected peak traffic; {{c2::stress}} = beyond capacity to find the breaking point and failure mode; {{c3::soak}} = sustained load for hours/days (leaks, exhaustion); {{c4::spike}} = sudden bursts.
notes.extra: Tools: k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust.

notes.back: SAST: analyse source without running it (Semgrep, CodeQL). DAST: attack the running app from outside (ZAP, Burp).
notes.extra: Add SCA for vulnerable dependencies and human pen testing.

notes.front: Fuzz testing, and what makes modern fuzzers effective?
notes.back: Feed huge volumes of random/mutated input to find crashes, hangs and memory bugs. Coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL, libFuzzer, Go fuzzing) evolve inputs that reach new code.
notes.analogy: Shaking a vending machine in every way possible to see what makes it jam.
notes.extra: Why it works: early experiments crashed or hung roughly a quarter to a third of UNIX utilities with random input.

notes.back: State a property that must hold for all inputs; the framework generates many inputs and shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample.
notes.analogy: Instead of testing a few chosen keys, you state "every key must open only its own lock" and let a machine try thousands.
notes.extra: Tools: QuickCheck (Haskell), Hypothesis (Python), fast-check (JS), jqwik (Java), proptest (Rust).

notes.back: A tool injects small faults (>→>=, drop a call) and reruns the suite. A surviving mutant reveals a gap in assertions.
notes.analogy: A fire drill for your test suite: start small fires and see whether the alarms go off.
notes.extra: Score = killed / total. Tools: PIT, Stryker, mutmut, cargo-mutants.

notes.front: Why does mutation testing work? (two hypotheses)
notes.back: Competent programmer: real faults are small deviations from correct code. Coupling effect: tests that catch simple faults also catch most complex ones.
Skilled, unscripted testing where learning, design and execution happen together, guided by a charter and time-boxed sessions.
notes.extra: Example charter: "explore checkout with expired cards to discover pricing errors". Finds bugs scripts didn't imagine.

notes.back: Screenshot diffs against baselines catch layout changes, but need stable rendering (fonts, animations, data) or they drown in noise.

notes.front: Why can't accessibility testing be fully automated?
notes.back: Automated scanners (axe) catch only about a third of WCAG issues; the rest need keyboard-only and screen-reader testing.
Canaries, feature flags, dark launches/shadow traffic, A/B tests, synthetic monitoring, chaos experiments. Requires good observability and fast rollback.
Deliberately injecting failures (killed instances, latency, outages) into production-like systems to verify resilience before real incidents do.
notes.analogy: A vaccine for systems: a controlled dose of failure builds resilience before the real infection.
notes.extra: Popularised by Netflix's Chaos Monkey.

notes.back: Alpha: internal users in a controlled environment. Beta: real external users in real environments before GA.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.text: FIRST properties of good unit tests: {{c1::Fast}}, {{c2::Independent}}, {{c3::Repeatable}}, {{c4::Self-validating}} (pass/fail without human judgement), {{c5::Timely}} (written with the code).

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: Set up state, perform one action, check the outcome. Maps 1:1 to Given / When / Then.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: Tests coupled to internals (private methods, call order, exact mock calls) break on harmless refactors. Test through public interfaces and observable outcomes.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.text: Test doubles: a {{c1::dummy}} is passed but never used; a {{c2::stub}} returns canned answers; a {{c3::spy}} is a stub that also records calls; a {{c4::mock}} is pre-programmed with expectations and verifies interactions; a {{c5::fake}} is a working lightweight implementation (in-memory DB).
notes.extra: Terms from Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: A stub only feeds answers (you then assert on state); a mock verifies that the expected calls happened (behaviour verification).
notes.analogy: A stub is a cardboard cut-out receptionist; a mock is an inspector checking you signed in correctly.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.front: Why "don't mock what you don't own"?
notes.back: A mock of a third-party API encodes your possibly wrong assumptions. Wrap it in your own adapter, mock the adapter, and integration-test the adapter for real.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: Classicist: real collaborators where cheap, verify state. Mockist: outside-in, mock collaborators, verify interactions; shapes interfaces early but couples tests to implementation.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: Red: write a small failing test. Green: simplest code to pass. Refactor: clean up with tests green. Repeat in small steps.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.front: Why must you see a new test fail first?
notes.back: A test that passes before the code exists may not exercise it (wrong target, missing assertion). Red proves it can detect the missing behaviour.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.front: Approval / snapshot / golden-master testing: use and risk?
notes.back: Capture output once, have a human approve it, diff future runs against it. Great for complex output and legacy code; risk: blind re-approval of diffs.

notes.deck: Software Testing::03 Unit Tests, Doubles & TDD
notes.back: A test that pins down what legacy code currently does (right or wrong) so you can change it safely.
notes.analogy: Photograph the room before renovating, so you can tell what you changed.
notes.extra: From Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code.

notes.back: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration/service tests, very few UI/E2E tests. Inverted = the ice-cream cone (slow, flaky, expensive).
notes.extra: Mike Cohn.

notes.front: Testing trophy: how does it differ from the pyramid, and why?
notes.back: Static analysis base, thin unit layer, large integration layer, small E2E top. For typical web apps, integration tests give the best confidence per cost.
notes.extra: Kent C. Dodds.

notes.text: Agile Testing Quadrants: Q1 {{c1::technology-facing, supports the team}} (unit, component); Q2 {{c2::business-facing, supports the team}} (functional, story/example tests); Q3 {{c3::business-facing, critiques the product}} (exploratory, usability, UAT); Q4 {{c4::technology-facing, critiques the product}} (performance, security, "-ilities").

notes.front: What does a healthy test portfolio look like?
notes.back: Fast deterministic tests at the bottom, a solid integration layer, contract tests between services, few critical-path E2E, then exploratory testing and production monitoring.
notes.extra: Pyramid vs trophy depends on the architecture.

notes.text: Coverage criteria, weakest to strongest: {{c1::statement/line}} → {{c2::branch/decision}} → condition → {{c3::MC/DC}} (required for top-level avionics software, DO-178C) → {{c4::path}} (usually infeasible).

notes.front: Why is code coverage a poor target?
notes.back: It proves a line ran, not that anything was asserted (Goodhart's law). Use it to find untested code; mutation score is the stronger signal.
notes.analogy: Counting the rooms a security guard walked through, not whether he checked any locks.

notes.front: Flaky test, and why must it be fixed fast?
notes.back: A test that passes and fails without code changes. Flakiness destroys trust: people start ignoring red builds. Quarantine and fix.
notes.analogy: A smoke alarm that goes off at random: soon everyone pulls the battery, and then the real fire goes unnoticed.
notes.extra: Causes: sleeps/timing, order dependence, shared state, network, unseeded randomness, clocks/time zones, concurrency.

notes.back: A test whose dependencies are all contained and controlled (no real network, shared DB or wall clock), so results depend only on the code under test.
notes.analogy: A sealed lab experiment: no outside air, so any change in the result comes from what you changed.

notes.front: Google test sizes: what defines small / medium / large?
notes.back: Resource limits, not scope. Small: one process, no I/O or sleeps. Medium: one machine, localhost network. Large: multiple machines/real systems.
"If you liked it, you should have put a test on it": if an infra change breaks behaviour you didn't test, that's on you.

notes.front: How do you keep a test suite fast?
notes.back: Push most tests to small/unit level, fake slow dependencies, parallelise, poll instead of sleep, and run slow suites (mutation, soak, full E2E) nightly.

notes.front: Where should mutation testing run in a pipeline?
notes.back: Nightly or post-merge, or incrementally on changed code only; full runs are too slow for every merge request.
A collaboration practice: discover behaviour through conversations and concrete examples, formulate them as scenarios, then automate them. The conversation is the main value.
People learning TDD got stuck on test vocabulary (what to test, where to start, what to call it); describing behaviour answered those questions.
notes.extra: Dan North, "Introducing BDD".

notes.text: The three BDD practices: {{c1::Discovery}} (collaborative conversations, e.g. Example Mapping) → {{c2::Formulation}} (examples written as Gherkin scenarios) → {{c3::Automation}} (step definitions make them executable).

notes.back: Business, development and testing perspectives meeting before implementation to examine a story and agree on examples and acceptance criteria.

notes.text: Example Mapping cards: {{c1::yellow}} = story, {{c2::blue}} = rules (acceptance criteria), {{c3::green}} = examples, {{c4::red}} = open questions.
notes.extra: Many reds → story not ready; many blues → story too big.

notes.back: Concrete, collaboratively refined examples as the single source of truth for requirements, tests and docs ("living documentation").
Given = context/precondition. When = the single action or event. Then = observable outcome. One When per scenario.

notes.front: Gherkin: which construct runs one scenario over a table of variations?
notes.back: Scenario Outline (Scenario Template) with an Examples table.
notes.extra: Use only for genuinely tabular variations of one rule.

notes.back: Declarative: say what the user achieves ("When Sam logs in"), not clicks. UI detail lives in step definitions, so scenarios survive UI changes.
Multi-rule scenarios are long, hard to name, fail for ambiguous reasons and hide which rule broke. Split by rule.

notes.text: Gherkin smells besides imperative steps: {{c1::incidental details}} (irrelevant IDs, timestamps), {{c2::vague scenarios without concrete data}}, and {{c3::generic actors}} ("the user") instead of personas.

notes.back: Chained scenarios fail in cascades, can't run in parallel or alone, and hide the real cause. Each scenario sets up its own Given.
Shared Givens run before every scenario in a feature. Pitfall: a long Background hides context the reader needs.

notes.front: Does BDD require Cucumber or UI tests?
notes.back: No. Scenarios can be automated at any layer; most teams run them against the domain/API and only a few through the UI.

notes.front: How do BDD and TDD fit together?
notes.back: Double loop: an outer failing acceptance scenario drives inner red-green-refactor unit cycles until it passes.
notes.analogy: The outer loop is the destination on the map; the inner loops are each turn of the steering wheel.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.back: Split inputs into classes the program should treat the same; test one representative per class, including invalid ones.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.back: Bugs cluster at partition edges (off-by-one, < vs <=): test at, just below and just above each boundary.
notes.analogy: Fence posts: the mistakes happen at the ends of the fence, not in the middle.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.front: Decision table testing: what does it reveal?
notes.back: Each combination of conditions → expected action becomes a test; gaps and contradictions in business rules become visible.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.back: Model states and events; test valid transitions, invalid ones (ship a cancelled order), sequences and loops. Missing arrows are often bugs.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.back: Most interaction bugs involve just two parameters, so covering every pair of values catches them with far fewer tests (310 combos → ~15–20).
notes.analogy: Seating plan for a dinner: make sure every pair of guests has met once, rather than trying every seating arrangement.
notes.extra: Tools: PICT, AllPairs.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.front: Error guessing, and how do past incidents feed it?
notes.back: Use known fault patterns (null, empty, duplicates, concurrency, encoding) to predict defects. Mine incidents for recurring categories and add them to a team checklist.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: ZOMBIES order for test-driving: {{c1::Zero}}, {{c2::One}}, {{c3::Many}}, {{c4::Boundaries}}, {{c5::Interface}}, {{c6::Exceptions}}, {{c7::Simple}} scenarios/solutions.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: CORRECT boundary checklist: {{c1::Conformance}} (format), {{c2::Ordering}}, {{c3::Range}}, {{c4::Reference}} (external dependencies), {{c5::Existence}} (null/empty), {{c6::Cardinality}} (0, 1, many), {{c7::Time}} (order, timeouts, zones).

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Right-BICEP: are the results {{c1::Right}}? {{c2::Boundary}} conditions, {{c3::Inverse}} relationships, {{c4::Cross-check}} by other means, force {{c5::Error}} conditions, {{c6::Performance}} within bounds.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: String edge cases: empty and whitespace-only, very long, {{c1::Unicode}} (emoji, combining and zero-width chars, RTL), {{c2::normalization}} (é as one vs two code points), {{c3::case folding}} (Turkish İ), injection characters, null bytes.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Numeric edge cases: 0, ±1, {{c1::min/max and overflow}}, {{c2::NaN, ±Infinity, -0.0}}, floating-point rounding (0.1+0.2), {{c3::money in floats}} (use decimals/minor units), division by zero.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Date/time edge cases: {{c1::DST gaps and overlaps}}, half-hour UTC offsets, {{c2::leap years}} (2100 isn't one), {{c3::month-end arithmetic}} (Jan 31 + 1 month), 2038 epoch overflow, clock skew.
notes.extra: Inject a clock; never call "now" directly.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Collection edge cases: empty, {{c1::one element}}, duplicates, already/reverse sorted, nulls, {{c2::mutation during iteration}}, {{c3::pagination boundaries}} (exactly page size, page size + 1).

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Distributed-system edge cases: timeouts and {{c1::retries without idempotency}} (duplicate delivery), {{c2::out-of-order messages}}, partial failure and partitions, {{c3::slow (not dead) dependencies}}, races, clock skew, stale caches.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Security edge cases: {{c1::IDOR}} (another tenant's ID), unauthenticated calls, {{c2::expired or forged tokens}}, oversized payloads, {{c3::path traversal}} (../), injection, rate limits.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.text: Property-based test patterns: {{c1::round-trip}} (decode(encode(x)) == x), {{c2::invariants}} (sort keeps length), {{c3::idempotence}} (f(f(x)) == f(x)), {{c4::oracle/differential}} (compare to a simple reference), "hard to compute, easy to verify".

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.back: When there's no oracle, check relations between outputs of related inputs: results for "A AND B" ⊆ results for "A".
notes.analogy: You can't know the true weight of a parcel, but you know adding a brick must make it heavier.

notes.deck: Software Testing::06 Test Design & Edge Cases
notes.front: Shrinking in property-based testing: why does it matter?
notes.back: The framework reduces a failing input to a minimal case ([0, -1] instead of 300 elements), making the root cause obvious.

notes.front: What makes a good test or scenario name?
notes.back: It states the behaviour and expected outcome ("expired card is declined at checkout"); a failure name alone tells you what broke.
notes.extra: A feature's scenario names should read like a specification.

notes.front: Why one logical assertion (behaviour) per test?
notes.back: Failures point to one behaviour and tests stay short. Several asserts on one outcome are fine; several behaviours are not.
Tests favour DAMP (Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases): some duplication is fine if each test reads standalone. Extract helpers for noise, not logic.

notes.front: Why avoid loops and conditionals in tests?
notes.back: Test logic can have bugs and often mirrors the implementation, so both share the mistake. Use literal expected values or parameterised cases.
Expected value computed the same way as the code (or asserting what a mock was told to return): it can never fail for a real bug.
notes.analogy: Copying the answer key from your own answers, then marking yourself 100%.
notes.extra: Very common in AI-generated tests.

notes.back: Factories with sensible defaults so each test sets only relevant fields (anOrder().withExpiredCard().build()), keeping incidental detail out.

notes.front: Every bug fix should start with…?
notes.back: A failing test that reproduces the bug: it proves you understood it, verifies the fix and becomes a regression test.

notes.front: How do you make time and randomness testable?
notes.back: Inject a clock and a seeded random source instead of global now()/random(); log seeds on failure.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Single most important practice when working with coding agents?
notes.back: Give the agent a pass/fail way to verify its own work (tests, build, linter, screenshot diff). Otherwise "looks done" is the stopping signal and you are the verifier.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: What does "use red/green TDD" mean as an agent prompt, and why is the red step crucial?
notes.back: Write tests first, run them and confirm they fail, then implement. Agents readily write tests that already pass, a false green.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: How should you prompt an agent to fix a bug?
notes.back: Give symptom, likely location and what "fixed" means; have it write a failing reproducing test, fix the root cause (not suppress it), and show passing output.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.text: Gating an agent's "done", soft to hard: {{c1::instruction in the prompt}} ("run tests and iterate") → evaluator re-checks a session goal → {{c2::deterministic hook}} (e.g. Stop hook blocks until the script passes) → {{c3::verification subagent}} that tries to refute the result.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why are hooks better than CLAUDE.md instructions for test discipline?
notes.back: Instructions are advisory and get lost in long context; hooks run deterministically every time.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.back: A separate model instance with its own context and limited tools whose only job is to check (and try to refute) the main agent's result, so the worker isn't grading itself.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why should a different agent/session review or test the implementation?
notes.back: A fresh context sees only the diff and criteria, not the reasoning behind them, so it's less biased toward the code.
notes.extra: Patterns: writer/reviewer sessions; one instance writes tests, another the code.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.back: Asked for gaps, they report some even for sound work; chasing all causes over-engineering. Restrict findings to correctness and stated requirements.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Key rule to stop agents gaming the tests?
notes.back: Don't let one agent modify both the tests and the code under test in the same task; human-approved tests are the spec.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.text: Agents reward-hack test suites by {{c1::deleting or skipping failing tests}}, {{c2::weakening assertions}}, {{c3::special-casing test inputs / hardcoding outputs}}, swallowing exceptions, or mocking away the thing under test.
notes.extra: Review test diffs as carefully as code diffs.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why is coverage especially misleading for AI-generated tests?
notes.back: Agents quickly produce high-coverage all-green suites whose assertions catch nothing; only mutation testing shows the suite would notice a regression.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Rule: "no generated test enters the suite without…"
notes.back: …proving it can fail: mutate the code under test (by hand or tool) and check the test goes red.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.back: Tests generated by the model that wrote the code share its blind spots, so they confirm rather than challenge it.
notes.analogy: Letting a student write and mark their own exam.
notes.extra: Mitigate: human examples, property tests, mutation testing, independent reviewers.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.back: The agent exercises the code like a human would (python -c, curl a dev server, browser automation); often reveals what tests missed.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why ask agents for evidence rather than claims of success?
notes.back: "Tests pass" is a claim; the command and its output or a screenshot is evidence, faster to review and usable for unattended runs.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: How do you prepare a large agentic task for verification?
notes.back: Have the agent interview you on edge cases, write a self-contained SPEC (files, interfaces, out of scope, an end-to-end check), then implement in a fresh session.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why agree on "what red looks like" in the plan before an agent codes?
notes.back: Naming the failing tests up front captures most of TDD's value before any code exists, and catches misunderstandings cheaply.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: How does a unit test act as a prompt for an agent?
notes.back: A behaviour-named test plus examples is a precise, checkable spec; one behaviour at a time keeps the model on narrow goals.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why are BDD scenarios good prompts for coding agents?
notes.back: They are natural-language, executable acceptance criteria: intent plus a pass/fail check. Humans own the scenarios; the agent implements.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: What test content belongs in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md?
notes.back: Exact test commands (incl. single test), runners, test-first rule, what "done" means, conventions. Keep it short; enforce must-always rules with hooks.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Why write characterization tests before an agent refactors legacy code?
notes.back: They lock in current behaviour so the refactor can be verified mechanically; otherwise there's no oracle and changes go unnoticed.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.back: FAIL_TO_PASS: failed before, must pass after (the fix works). PASS_TO_PASS: passed before, must still pass (no regressions).
notes.extra: A good acceptance model for any agent task.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: How do you test features that call an LLM?
notes.back: Evals: curated inputs with expected properties, deterministic checks where possible, calibrated LLM-as-judge rubrics, repeated runs, tracked like a regression suite.

notes.deck: Software Testing::08 Testing with Coding Agents
notes.front: Does AI-assisted development reduce the need for testing discipline?
notes.back: No, AI amplifies existing practices: strong test feedback lets agents iterate autonomously; weak suites let them ship plausible wrong code faster.
